citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $w_{ij}=w_{ji}\ge0$ and $w_{ii}=0$. Define $d_i=\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, and $L=D-W$. The support graph has vertex set $V$ and edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$; isolated vertices are singleton connected components. Put $V_+=\{i\in V:d_i>0\}$, let $D_+$ and $L_+$ be the principal submatrices indexed by $V_+$, and, only when $V_+\ne\varnothing$, define $L_{\mathrm{sym},+}=D_+^{-1/2}L_+D_+^{-1/2}$ on $\mathbb R^{V_+}$.

Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, and zero-diagonal. Put $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, and $L=D-W$. The support graph has edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$; two vertices lie in the same connected component exactly when a finite path of support edges joins them; connected components include isolated singleton vertices. Let $B\subseteq V$ be nonempty, put $U=V\setminus B$, and prescribe $y_B\in\mathbb R^B$. Call the boundary anchored when every connected component meeting $U$ also meets $B$. For $f\in\mathbb R^V$ with $f|_B=y_B$, define the Dirichlet graph energy $E(f)=\tfrac12 f^TLf$. A function is harmonic on $U$ when $(Lf)_u=0$ for every $u\in U$. A graph-harmonic label extension is any minimizer of $E$ over the affine set of functions with the prescribed boundary values; the definition itself makes no uniqueness assertion.

Let $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$, let $W$ be symmetric, nonnegative, and zero-diagonal, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sum_jw_{ij})$, let $L=D-W$, and let the support graph have edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$. For every $f\in\mathbb R^n$, $$f^TLf=\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2.$$ Consequently $L$ is positive semidefinite and $$\ker L=\{f\in\mathbb R^n:f\text{ is constant on each connected component of the support graph}\},$$ including isolated singleton components.

Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

1. If $L\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal, the forward
   substitution recursion of
   [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] produces the
   unique solution of $Lx=b$.
2. If $U\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, the backward
   substitution recursion produces the unique solution of $Ux=b$.

Each solve uses exactly $n$ divisions,
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiplications, and $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ additions or
subtractions, hence $O(n^2)$ scalar operations.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite and let
$A=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal.

1. For every right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$, the system $Ax=b$ is solved by
   first solving $Ly=b$ and then solving $L^*x=y$.
2. The two triangular solves cost $2n^2+O(n)$ scalar operations altogether, and
   the dense Cholesky factorisation costs
   $$\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   scalar operations, compared with
   $$\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   for dense LU factorisation without exploiting symmetry.

derivations.claim: If $U=\varnothing$, then $B=V$ and the affine set of extensions contains only $f=y_B$. It is therefore the unique minimizer; the maximum and minimum assertions over $U$ are vacuous, and the one-hot boundary rows are in $\Delta_C$.

Suppose $U\ne\varnothing$ and put $M=L_{UU}$. For nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^U$, extend $v$ by zero on $B$ to $\widetilde v\in\mathbb R^V$. By [F3], $v^TMv=\widetilde v^TL\widetilde v=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(\widetilde v_i-\widetilde v_j)^2$. If this sum were zero, every positive-weight edge would have equal endpoint values, so $\widetilde v$ would be constant on each support component. Every component meeting $U$ meets $B$, where $\widetilde v=0$, forcing $v=0$, a contradiction. Thus $M$ is positive definite; it is symmetric as a principal block of the symmetric matrix $L$.

By [F5], $M$ has a Cholesky factorization $M=RR^T$ with positive diagonal. By [F6] and [F7], solving $Rv=-L_{UB}y_B$ and then $R^Tz=v$ gives a unique vector $z=-M^{-1}L_{UB}y_B$ in finitely many scalar operations.

Let $f_B=y_B$ and $f_U=z$. For any $h\in\mathbb R^U$, block expansion and $Mz+L_{UB}y_B=0$ give $E(f+h)-E(f)=h^T(Mz+L_{UB}y_B)+\tfrac12h^TMh=\tfrac12h^TMh$. This is positive for $h\ne0$ by step 1.2, so $f$ is the unique minimizer and has the stated block formula.

The equation solved in step 2.1 gives $(Lf)_u=0$ for every $u\in U$. If $d_u=0$, then $u$ is an isolated support component contained in $U$, contradicting anchoring; hence $d_u>0$ and $f_u=\sum_jw_{uj}f_j/d_u$, a weighted average of neighboring values.

Let $m=\max_{i\in V}f_i$. If $m>\max_{b\in B}y_b$, then no maximizing vertex lies in $B$, so choose a maximizing vertex $u_0\in U$. At $u_0$, the weighted-average equation in step 3.2 and $f_j\le m$ force $f_j=m$ for each neighbor with positive weight. Choose a shortest finite path in its support component to $B$; every interior vertex lies in $U$, so applying the same argument successively forces the boundary value at the end of the path to equal $m$, a contradiction. Therefore $\max_{i\in V}f_i\le\max_{b\in B}y_b$.

Apply step 4.1 to $-f$, whose boundary values are $-y_B$ and whose unlabeled coordinates satisfy the same weighted-average equations. This yields $\min_{b\in B}y_b\le f_u$ for every $u\in U$, completing the maximum-principle bounds.

For one-hot boundary data, let $f^{(c)}$ be the minimizer for coordinate $c$ and put $g=\sum_{c=1}^C f^{(c)}$. By step 2.1 each coordinate satisfies $(Lf^{(c)})_u=0$, and by steps 4.1 and 5.1 each $f^{(c)}_u$ is between 0 and 1. Linearity gives $(Lg)_u=0$ on $U$, while the one-hot boundary data give $g|_B=1$. The constant-one function also has these properties because every row sum of $L=D-W$ is zero. The difference $h=g-\mathbf1$ therefore has $h|_B=0$ and $L_{UU}h_U=0$; positive definiteness from step 1.2 forces $h_U=0$. Thus $g$ is identically 1, so every unlabeled row lies in $\Delta_C$.

citations.quote: A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: For each $j$, assigning mass $\mu(x)$ to $(x,h_j(x))$ defines a probability law because the masses are nonnegative and sum to one. The feature marginal is $\mu$ for both laws, and $h_0=h_1$ on $\mathcal S$, so the observed labeled input and unlabeled marginal are identical. Finiteness and the discrete sigma-algebra make every predictor and zero-one loss measurable, so [F2] gives the risk formula in the Statement.

Fix $g\in\mathcal H$. At each $x
e x_\star$, the two risk summands agree because $h_0(x)=h_1(x)$. At $x_\star$, the binary labels differ, so exactly one of the two indicators $\mathbf1\{g(x_\star)
e h_0(x_\star)\}$ and $\mathbf1\{g(x_\star)
e h_1(x_\star)\}$ equals one. Therefore $R_{P_0}(g)+R_{P_1}(g)\ge q$.

Multiply the inequality in step 2.1 by $Q(g)\ge0$ and sum over the finite class $\mathcal H$. Since $\sum_gQ(g)=1$, the two expected risks sum to at least $q$, so at least one is at least $q/2$. This proves the claimed maximum.

citations.quote:
Let $q\ge2$, let $\mathcal C=\{1,\ldots,q\}$, and let $(\mathcal X,d)$ be a finite metric space, meaning $d:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ is symmetric, $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ for all $x,y,z$. The input is a nonempty ordered list $S_0=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^m$ of labeled examples with $y_i\in\mathcal C$, a finite ordered set $U_0\subseteq\mathcal X\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ of unlabeled examples, an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le m$, a confidence threshold $\tau\in[1/q,1]$, a pseudo-label weight $\lambda>0$, and a round cap $T\in\mathbb N_0$. A true labeled record has weight $1$; a pseudo-labeled record has weight $\lambda$.

Maintain an ordered training list $R_t$, initially $S_0$, a remaining unlabeled set $U_t$, initially $U_0$, and an initially empty pseudo-label log. To predict at $x\in U_t$, order all records $(x_i,y_i,w_i)\in R_t$ by increasing $(d(x,x_i),i)$, where $i$ is their stable record index, and take the first $k$ records $N_t(x)$. For $c\in\mathcal C$, put $V_{t,c}(x)=\sum_{(x_i,y_i,w_i)\in N_t(x)}w_i\mathbf 1\{y_i=c\}$. Let $\widehat y_t(x)$ be the smallest class index attaining $\max_c V_{t,c}(x)$, and define confidence $\kappa_t(x)=\max_c V_{t,c}(x)/\sum_cV_{t,c}(x)$. The denominator is positive because $k\ge1$ and every record weight is positive.

If $U_0=\varnothing$, set status $\texttt{no-unlabeled-inputs}$ and skip the round loop. Otherwise, for rounds $t=0,\ldots,T-1$, compute all predictions from the same current list $R_t$. Let $A_t=\{x\in U_t:\kappa_t(x)\ge\tau\}$. If $A_t=\varnothing$, set status $\texttt{no-additions}$ and leave the loop. Otherwise append one pseudo-labeled record for each $x\in A_t$, in the supplied order on $U_0$, using its predicted class and weight $\lambda$; append $(t,x,\widehat y_t(x),\lambda)$ to the pseudo-label log, and remove all points in $A_t$ from $U_t$. A pseudo-label is never revised. If the updated $U_t=\varnothing$, set status $\texttt{all-labelled}$ and leave the loop. If all $T$ rounds finish without an earlier stop and points remain in $U_t$, set status $\texttt{round-cap}$; this includes the case $T=0$.

For any query $x\in\mathcal X$, define the returned classifier by the same nearest-record ordering and weighted vote using the final training list, with the smallest-index vote tie rule. In every case return that classifier, the pseudo-label log, the remaining unlabeled set, and the status. The procedure makes no population-risk or pseudo-label-correctness guarantee.

Since the confidence meets the threshold, the algorithm appends pseudo-label $(5,1)$ with weight $1$ and removes 5 from the unlabeled set. The output status is all-labelled, and the no-relabel rule retains the pseudo-label 1 even though the specified true label is 2.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty feature set with its discrete sigma-algebra, and let $\mu:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)=1$. Let $\mathcal S\subsetneq\mathcal X$ be a nonempty set of observed labeled inputs, and choose $x_\star\in\mathcal X\setminus\mathcal S$ with $q=\mu(x_\star)>0$. Let $h_0,h_1:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$ agree on $\mathcal X\setminus\{x_\star\}$ and differ at $x_\star$. For $j\in\{0,1\}$, let $P_j$ be the joint law assigning mass $\mu(x)$ to $(x,h_j(x))$. Both laws have the same feature marginal and the same observed labels on $\mathcal S$. Let $\mathcal H=\{g:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}\}$, and let $Q:\mathcal H\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{g\in\mathcal H}Q(g)=1$, so it is a probability vector; take the same $Q$ under both laws, as a predictor rule using their common information must do. For the zero-one population risk
$$R_{P_j}(g)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\mathbf 1\{g(x)\ne h_j(x)\},$$
the expected risks satisfy
$$\max_{j\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{g\in\mathcal H}Q(g)R_{P_j}(g)\ge\frac q2.$$

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Here the unseen atom is $b$ and $q=P_X(b)=1/2$. The two laws agree at the observed point $a$ and have the same $P_X$, so the theorem in [F1] applies and gives a maximum expected risk of at least $q/2=1/4$.

Directly, let $p=Q\{g\in\mathcal H:g(b)=1\}$. The two expected risks have the same nonnegative contribution from $a$. Their contributions at $b$ are respectively $p/2$ under $P_0$ and $(1-p)/2$ under $P_1$, so their sum is at least $1/2$ and their maximum is at least $1/4$.

For $f\in\mathbb R^V$ with $f|_B=y_B$, define the Dirichlet graph energy $E(f)=\tfrac12 f^TLf$. A function is harmonic on $U$ when $(Lf)_u=0$ for every $u\in U$. A graph-harmonic label extension is any minimizer of $E$ over the affine set of functions with the prescribed boundary values; the definition itself makes no uniqueness assertion.

Inputs are $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, a matrix $W\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, a nonempty labeled subset $B\subseteq V$, a boundary-label matrix $Y_B\in\mathbb R^{|B|\times r}$ with $r\ge1$, an operation cap $K\in\mathbb N_0$ per label coordinate, and a residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. Use exact real arithmetic in the mathematical specification. Reject with status $\texttt{invalid-input}$ unless $W$ is symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, and zero-diagonal. Set $U=V\setminus B$, $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, and $L=D-W$. The support graph has edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$; two vertices are in the same connected component exactly when a finite path of support edges joins them. Use increasing vertex order for every submatrix, boundary vector, and returned output coordinate.

Inspect every connected component in increasing vertex order. If some component meeting $U$ misses $B$, return status $\texttt{unanchored-component}$ and the unanchored components before forming a solve. If $U=\varnothing$, return $Y_B$, an empty unlabeled output, and status $\texttt{no-unlabeled-vertices}$. Otherwise set $M=L_{UU}$.

For each column $c=1,\ldots,r$ in order, start a fresh counter at zero and form $b_c=-L_{UB}(Y_B)_{:,c}$, evaluating the matrix-vector product in increasing vertex order. Recompute a fresh lower-triangular Cholesky factor $R$ of $M$ for this column by the recurrence: initialize $R$ to zero; in increasing order $j=1,\ldots,|U|$, compute $p_j=M_{jj}-\sum_{k<j}R_{jk}^2$, return status $\texttt{factorization-failure}$ if $p_j\le0$, set $R_{jj}=\sqrt{p_j}$, and for $i>j$ set $R_{ij}=(M_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}R_{ik}R_{jk})/R_{jj}$. Recompute $R$ for each column so that the factorization cost is part of that column's cap.

Count each real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, comparison, and square root as one scalar operation. Evaluate every finite sum left-to-right in increasing index order, with an empty sum equal to zero. For each coordinate of $b_c$, implement the unary negation as one subtraction from zero and include that subtraction in the count. Input validation, degree/Laplacian construction, component scans, loop-control comparisons, and budget checks are outside the per-column count. The count for column $c$ includes forming $b_c$, its Cholesky recurrence, both triangular substitutions, and its residual calculation. Before each counted operation, if it would make the counter exceed $K$, return status $\texttt{budget-exhausted}$ with outputs and residuals for only the fully completed columns before $c$. If a Cholesky pivot satisfies $p_j\le0$, return status $\texttt{factorization-failure}$ with outputs and residuals for only the fully completed columns before $c$.

Solve $Rv_c=b_c$ by $v_{c,i}=((b_c)_i-\sum_{j<i}R_{ij}v_{c,j})/R_{ii}$ in increasing $i$, and solve $R^Tz_c=v_c$ by $z_{c,i}=(v_{c,i}-\sum_{j>i}R_{ji}z_{c,j})/R_{ii}$ in decreasing $i$, using the same counter and sum convention. Compute $e_{c,i}=\sum_{j=1}^{|U|}M_{ij}z_{c,j}-(b_c)_i$ in increasing $i$, then $\rho_c=(\sum_{i=1}^{|U|}e_{c,i}^2)^{1/2}$, again using the same counter. If $\rho_c>\varepsilon$, return status $\texttt{residual-failure}$ with candidate coordinates and residuals through column $c$. If all columns pass, return $Y_U=(z_1,\ldots,z_r)$, the residuals, and status $\texttt{residual-passed}$.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: Induct on $j$. At $j=1$, testing $e_1$ in [A1] gives $p_1=M_{11}>0$. For $j>1$, suppose columns $1,\ldots,j-1$ have been computed with positive diagonal and let $T=R_{\{1,\ldots,j-1\},\{1,\ldots,j-1\}}$ and $A=M_{\{1,\ldots,j-1\},\{1,\ldots,j-1\}}$; the induction hypothesis gives $A=TT^T$. The block $A$ is positive definite because extending any nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ by zeros gives a nonzero vector to which [A1] applies. Its kernel is therefore zero; [F2] makes $A$ invertible. The lower-triangular matrix $T$ is invertible as well, since solving $Tx=0$ row by row with its positive diagonal forces every coordinate of $x$ to be zero. Put $m=(M_{1j},\ldots,M_{j-1,j})^T$ and $u=(R_{j1},\ldots,R_{j,j-1})^T$. The already computed recurrence at each column $i<j$ gives $M_{ij}=\sum_{k<i}R_{ik}R_{jk}+R_{ii}R_{ji}$, so $Tu=m$. Since $A=TT^T$, this implies $m^TA^{-1}m=u^Tu$. The leading $j\times j$ block $P$ of $M$ is positive definite by the same zero-extension argument. For the nonzero vector $(-A^{-1}m,1)$, its quadratic form under $P$ is $M_{jj}-m^TA^{-1}m=M_{jj}-u^Tu=p_j>0$. Thus $R_{jj}=\sqrt{p_j}$ is positive and every division defining $R_{ij}$ is by a positive number. The recurrence is well-defined through column $j$, and the same formulas give the factorization identity on the leading $j\times j$ block.

For every $j$, the pivot equation gives $M_{jj}=\sum_{k<j}R_{jk}^2+R_{jj}^2=(RR^T)_{jj}$. For every $i>j$, rearranging the recurrence gives $M_{ij}=\sum_{k<j}R_{ik}R_{jk}+R_{ij}R_{jj}=(RR^T)_{ij}$. These identities fill the diagonal and lower triangle; symmetry of $M$ and $RR^T$ fills the upper triangle. The initialized matrix remains lower triangular, and each diagonal entry is positive by step 1.1, so it is the required Cholesky factor.
